chat.author: Steve Traugott
chat.text: I also think it's helpful to think of all of this in terms of kept or broken reciprocal promises -- an HTTP server promises to serve X in return for the client promising to be well-behaved.  A client promises to be well-behaved in return for the delivered response.  Right now those promises are only implied at the protocol level.  So in practice right now, HTTP provides little accountability for a client breaking that promise.  Adding accountability means adding some sort of decentralized auth for what would otherwise be anonymous queries; those clients that are not able or willing to be held accountable will inevitably wind up in a slow lane, time-permitting response queue.

chat.author: Steve Traugott
chat.text:
Problems with trying to make a distinction between "fully automated crawlers" and "agents acting on behalf of individuals":  
(A) "Agent, please analyze every linked path at www.example.com" causes the same abuse as a cron job doing the same thing. 
(B) In the former case, the agent is doing a specific job tasked by a human, and in the latter case, the crawler is doing a specific job tasked by ...another human.    Trying to split those hairs too finely will lead to trying to discern people asking agents to do things as individuals vs as employees.
